title: What to introduce, and when
byline: There is no set calendar for which vegetable comes when. There is a good reason to bring in allergens early and keep them in the diet.
image_alt: Small bowls of egg, yogurt, pasta, fish, and peanut purée

findings.lead: ‘One new food at a time’ is a habit, not a rule.
findings.text: New allergens are easier to judge if they come one at a time. Everyday vegetables don’t need a three-day wait.

findings.lead: Gluten can come in with the first foods.
findings.text: Delaying it doesn’t prevent coeliac disease. Do avoid very large amounts in the first weeks.

findings.lead: Before one, cow’s milk isn’t the main drink.
findings.text: Small amounts in a sauce, in porridge, or as yogurt are fine from the start of solids.

sections.heading: Skip the long ladder
paragraphs: Older weaning charts added one new vegetable every few days and held back meat, wheat, egg, and fish until late in the first year. That made for tidy feeding diaries and poor iron intake. It also missed the window when introducing allergens early seems to protect.

Introduce one new common allergen on a morning when your baby is well: give a small amount and watch. You can repeat it the next day. Other new foods, like a different vegetable, can share the plate. If there’s no reaction, keep that allergen in the diet several times a week. One taste isn’t enough to maintain tolerance.

sections.heading: Gluten, egg, fish, and the rest
paragraphs: ESPGHAN says gluten can be introduced between 4 and 12 months, avoiding large amounts in the first weeks and throughout infancy. A portion of pasta or bread is fine. A pile of biscuits isn’t.

Cook egg all the way through. Fish should be boneless and fully cooked. Peanut and other nuts should be smooth butter, thinned into food: never whole, and never a thick spoonful. Sesame means tahini, not a sprinkle of whole seeds. You’ll find the details, and the plan for high-risk babies and peanut, on the allergen page.

sections.heading: Milk as a drink and milk as a food
paragraphs: Breast milk or infant formula stays the main drink until 12 months. Using whole cow’s milk as that drink raises the risk of low iron intake, and it’s no substitute for formula. After the first birthday, whole cow’s milk can become the main drink, at roughly 350 to 400 ml a day so it doesn’t crowd out meals.

Yogurt, small amounts of pasteurised cheese, and milk cooked into a sauce count as food, not drinks, and are fine from six months. Unpasteurised milk and mould-ripened or blue cheeses stay off the menu for the first few years.

title: Introducing allergens
byline: Delaying peanut, egg, and milk doesn’t prevent allergy. For most babies, the safer plan is to start them in a safe texture and keep them coming.
image_alt: Peanut yogurt, a set omelette, and smooth tahini

findings.lead: Start the common allergens when you start solids.
findings.text: For most babies that’s around six months, and never before four.

findings.lead: Regular peanut from infancy sharply reduced peanut allergy in high-risk children.
findings.text: In the LEAP trial, children with severe eczema or egg allergy had a relative reduction of about 80 percent by age five.

findings.lead: Some babies should only try peanut once a doctor agrees.
findings.text: That means babies with severe eczema, an existing egg allergy, or both. If your doctor is worried, don’t go ahead on your own.

findings.lead: Redness around the mouth isn’t anaphylaxis.
findings.text: Trouble breathing, floppiness, hives all over, or repeated vomiting after a food is an emergency.

sections.heading: What the evidence says now
paragraphs: For years, families were told to delay peanut, egg, and fish. Allergy rates kept rising under that advice, and it didn’t bring them down. ESPGHAN now says allergenic foods can be introduced when solids begin, any time after four months. For a healthy baby, in practice that means when solids start, around six months.

The foods worth planning for are peanut, egg, cow’s milk, wheat, sesame, fish, soy, and tree nuts. Shellfish can join the list once you’re ready to serve it fully cooked and finely chopped. Offer them as real food, not a hidden trace, and keep serving them.

sections.heading: LEAP, EAT, and the guidelines that followed
paragraphs: LEAP enrolled babies at high risk because of severe eczema, egg allergy, or both. Those who ate peanut regularly until age five were far less likely to develop peanut allergy than those who avoided it. The EAT trial offered six allergens from three months to breastfed babies from the general population. The protection was clearest in children who actually ate the foods often enough, which many families found hard to manage.

The US addendum guideline put LEAP into practice: for high-risk babies, peanut is considered between four and six months, once other solids show the baby is ready, often after testing. Babies with mild or moderate eczema are offered peanut around six months. Babies without eczema can have it along with everything else. European guidance points the same way.

sections.heading: The first tastes
paragraphs: Choose a morning when your child is well, not a vaccination day or a day with a fever. Offer a small amount of one new allergen and stay close. For peanut, the right texture is smooth peanut butter thinned into yogurt or fruit. A spoonful of thick peanut butter can block the airway. Baked egg and hard-boiled egg both count, as long as the white and yolk are set. For sesame, thin tahini into a dip.

If the first taste goes well, repeat it, and then keep it in the weekly routine. Stopping for months after one good taste is how a planned introduction quietly turns into avoidance. A baby with severe eczema or a known egg allergy should be assessed before trying peanut. That’s a doctor’s job, and it may involve a skin test or a supervised feed.

sections.heading: Rashes, illness, and emergencies
paragraphs: Drool plus a new acidic fruit often turns the chin red. That’s contact irritation; it fades and isn’t, on its own, a reason for allergy testing. Spreading hives, swollen lips or tongue, vomiting, a hoarse cry, wheezing, or a baby who turns pale and floppy needs emergency care. Antihistamine is not the treatment for breathing difficulty.

Don’t diagnose an allergy from one meal during an illness, and don’t start a brand-new allergen on a day your child is already unwell. After a true allergic reaction, keep the food out until a specialist has made a plan. Don’t try a challenge test at home.

title: Portions, texture, and milk
byline: Appetite is a better guide than counting spoonfuls. Milk stays the main drink until the first birthday.
image_alt: A small bowl of vegetable mash beside a glass of milk

findings.lead: Start with a few teaspoons, then follow your baby’s lead.
findings.text: A few spoonfuls one day and a whole bowl the next can both be normal.

findings.lead: Until 12 months, milk is still most of the diet.
findings.text: Food is there for iron and practice. It doesn’t need to replace milk feeds on a schedule you make up.

findings.lead: By eight or nine months, textures should be moving on.
findings.text: You can offer water from an open cup with meals. Not juice.

sections.heading: How much food?
paragraphs: The first meals are as much about practice as nutrition: one to three teaspoons, once a day, building up to two and then three meals. By the end of the first year, many children have three meals and two snacks, though portions still vary hugely from child to child and day to day.

Pushing those last few spoonfuls teaches a child to ignore feeling full. So does using food as a reward, or as comfort for every upset. There’s more on sharing responsibility on the meals page: you decide what to offer, your child decides how much to eat.

sections.heading: Where milk fits
paragraphs: Keep offering breast milk or formula on demand alongside meals. There’s no need to drop a milk feed the day solids start. As the first birthday approaches, food provides more of the iron, and milk feeds often settle into morning, evening, and maybe one more.
After 12 months, drinking well over 400 ml of milk a day is a common reason a toddler won’t eat. Offer water with meals. Sipping from a bottle all day can also leave milk pooling on the teeth.

sections.heading: Texture and cups
paragraphs: Smooth food at six months, mash and soft strips by eight or nine, and chopped family food by twelve is a good rough path. Some babies move faster, some slower. The real risk is a child who reaches one still on thin purée and then refuses lumps.

Offer sips of water from an open or free-flow cup at meals so your baby gets to practise drinking. Juice, even diluted, isn’t a drink for babies. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises no juice before 12 months.

title: A week, in outline
byline: These are examples, not rules. Swap in whichever iron food and allergen you’re working on.
image_alt: Porridge with apple, soft pasta with meat, and yogurt

findings.lead: At six months, portions are small and milk feeds carry on.
findings.text: One or two meals a day, each with an iron-rich food, is plenty to begin with.

findings.lead: At nine months, the focus is texture and keeping allergens regular.
findings.text: Three meals, soft finger foods, and peanut or egg on several days.

findings.lead: At twelve months, your child eats family food, with their portion unsalted.
findings.text: Milk becomes a drink from a cup, in moderate amounts.

sections.heading: Around six months
paragraphs: Breakfast could be oat porridge with cooked apple, with a teaspoon of smooth peanut butter stirred in once peanut has been tried. Lunch could be chicken, sweet potato, and broccoli, mashed. If your baby wants a second meal, try red lentil soup or egg mashed into vegetables.
Over the week, deliberately repeat egg, peanut, wheat, and a dairy food. Keep breast milk or formula as the main drink. Offer water, but don’t push it.

sections.heading: Around nine months
paragraphs: Breakfast: porridge or egg with fruit. Lunch: soft pasta with tomato and mince, or fish with rice and greens. Afternoon snack: yogurt or a soft vegetable fritter. Dinner can be the family’s stew, mashed, taken out before the salt goes in.
Finger foods go alongside the spoon: a strip of soft cooked pepper, a piece of ripe pear, a flake of salmon. If you haven’t already, this is the age to leave thin purée behind.

sections.heading: Around twelve months
paragraphs: Meals now look like everyone else’s. Bread and fruit for breakfast, a bean stew or pasta for lunch, baked egg or leftover meat in the evening. Snacks are fruit, yogurt, or a soft oat bite, not a sweet biscuit out of habit.

Honey is now considered safer as far as botulism goes, but it’s still a poor everyday sweetener. Keep halving grapes lengthways. Whole nuts are still years away. A little salt can go into family food; your child’s portion doesn’t need as much as an adult’s.

title: How mealtimes work
byline: What goes on the table is up to you. Whether your child eats it, and how much, is up to them. Pressure is a poor teacher.
image_alt: A plate of soft vegetables and rice with a spoon

findings.text: You choose the food, the time, and the place. Your child chooses whether to eat and how much.

findings.lead: A refused food usually needs more calm tries, not a replacement meal.
findings.text: It can take eight to fifteen pressure-free tastes to accept a new flavour, and that’s normal.

findings.lead: Screens, aeroplane spoons, and pudding bribes backfire.
findings.text: They teach children to ignore their hunger and to see sweet food as the prize.

sections.heading: Who decides what
paragraphs: Ellyn Satter’s division of responsibility is the clearest summary of responsive feeding. You offer a meal with some structure: something your child usually eats, and something they’re still getting to know. You sit down together. You don’t plead, chase them with the spoon, or cook a second lunch when the first is refused.
When a baby turns away, clamps their mouth shut, or starts playing, they’ve finished. Ending the meal then counts as a success. It’s how they learn that their own sense of fullness matters.

sections.heading: Try, try again
paragraphs: Food neophobia, a wariness of new foods, increases in the toddler years and is completely ordinary. What helps, according to the evidence, is calm, repeated exposure: the food appears, nobody makes a fuss, and it comes back next week. Praising eating and showing disappointment at refusal both add pressure.

Cooking to order, where a refusal brings out a favourite instead, teaches your child to refuse. Serve one meal. Include a ‘safe’ food so your child won’t leave hungry. Let the new food be something they’re free to ignore.

sections.heading: Tricks that are not worth it
paragraphs: Feeding while a screen distracts the baby fills the tummy but skips the learning. Bribes (‘finish this and you can have something sweet’) turn the savoury food into a chore. Hiding every vegetable so well that your child never sees one skips the learning too. A visible piece is doing its job even if it stays on the plate.
Eat together whenever you can. Children copy the people at the table far more reliably than they follow a talk about healthy food.

title: Gagging and choking
byline: Gagging is loud and helpful. Choking is silent and an emergency. Learn the first-aid response before you need it.
image_alt: Grapes cut lengthwise, cooked apple, and nut butter stirred into yogurt

findings.lead: Noise is reassuring. Silence is not.
findings.text: A gagging baby coughs, splutters, and goes red. A choking baby cannot cry or cough effectively.

findings.lead: Shape matters more than the food itself.
findings.text: Most choking in babies involves round, hard, sticky, or coin-shaped pieces.

findings.lead: Read up, then practise with a qualified instructor.
findings.text: Back blows and chest thrusts for babies are a physical skill. Reading a website isn’t practice.

sections.heading: How to tell them apart
paragraphs: In young babies, the gag reflex sits near the front of the tongue and moves back as they learn to eat. When food goes too far back, they gag noisily and the piece comes forward again. It’s scary to watch, but it usually means things are working as they should. Stay close, stay calm, and let your baby deal with it. While they’re still coughing well, don’t turn them upside down or poke around blindly in their mouth.

Choking means the airway is blocked. The baby is silent or makes only a weak sound, can’t cough, and may turn blue. That’s an emergency. The standard response for babies is alternating back blows and chest thrusts, then calling emergency services. Take a course with the Hungarian Red Cross or similar, and keep a trusted illustrated guide saved. Don’t rely on this paragraph in the moment.

sections.heading: Shapes to change
paragraphs: Cut grapes, cherry tomatoes, and round slices of sausage lengthways. Cook apple until soft instead of giving hard raw pieces. Skip popcorn, whole nuts, hard sweets, sticky marshmallows, and crisps. Always thin nut butter into food; never leave it as a lump on a spoon. Meat should be tender, not a cube your baby has to gnaw.
Sit your baby upright in a high chair for every meal. Eating in a car seat, on the go, or leaning back makes it harder to cough food clear. Stay in the room.

sections.heading: Where to learn first aid
paragraphs: The NHS and the British Red Cross both publish step-by-step guides to infant choking, and the Hungarian Red Cross teaches first aid in person. A guide helps you understand the steps; a class helps your hands remember them.
The BLISS trial is why finger foods aren’t off limits. It isn’t a reason to skip the class: the families in that trial were taught which foods to avoid.
